Joshua 1.audience: The LORD speaks to Joshua after Moses' death, and Joshua addresses the officers and the eastern tribes—Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh—who had already received land (Joshua 1:12–15).

culture.title: Meditating on the book
culture.text: The book of the law was a written scroll. In the ancient world, people usually read aloud, even to themselves; the Hebrew word translated "meditate" can mean to murmur or speak quietly.

culture.title: Three days' preparation
culture.text: The people prepared food for the crossing. Manna continued until they ate the produce of the land (Joshua 5:12).

Joshua 2.audience: Israel remembered Rahab as a Canaanite who sheltered the spies and joined Israel; the text says she lived among them "even unto this day" (Joshua 6:25). She appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

culture.title: Houses on the wall
culture.text: Some cities had houses built into or against their walls. Rahab's window opened onto the outside of the wall, so she could let the spies down by a cord.

culture.title: Flax on the roof
culture.text: Flax stalks were laid out on flat roofs to dry before being processed into linen. Rahab hides the spies under them.

culture.title: Jericho
culture.text: Jericho is an oasis city near the Jordan, fed by a strong spring. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited sites in the world and guarded the route into the hill country.

Joshua 3.audience: Israel crosses the Jordan "at the time of harvest," when the river overflowed its banks (Joshua 3:15). Hearers knew the Jordan's spring flood season.

culture.title: The Jordan in flood
culture.text: Melting snow from Mount Hermon and spring rains raised the Jordan in March–April, the barley harvest season. The waters stopped at the city of Adam, about 18 miles upstream (Joshua 3:16).

culture.title: Following the ark at a distance
culture.text: The people kept about 2,000 cubits (roughly 3,000 feet) behind the ark.

Joshua 4.audience: The twelve stones set up at Gilgal were a memorial for later children who would ask, "What mean these stones?" (Joshua 4:21). Gilgal remained an important place in Israel (1 Samuel 11:15).

culture.title: Memorial stones
culture.text: Piles of stones or standing stones marked important events and places. Jacob and Laban's heap of witness is another example (Genesis 31:46–48).

Joshua 5.audience: The men born in the wilderness had not been circumcised. Israel's first acts in the land are circumcision and the Passover at Gilgal, on the plains of Jericho.

culture.title: Flint knives
culture.text: Sharp knives of flint were used for circumcision long after metal tools were common (also Exodus 4:25). Flint can be made sharper than early bronze blades.

culture.title: The end of manna
culture.text: Israel ate parched (roasted) grain and unleavened cakes from the land's produce, and the manna stopped the next day.

Joshua 6.audience: Israel heard the fall of Jericho as the LORD's victory, not their own. Hebrews remembers it as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:30).

culture.title: Rams' horn trumpets
culture.text: The shofar was made from a ram's horn. It was blown for signals in war and on holy days and is still used in synagogues today.

culture.title: Devoted to destruction
culture.text: Jericho was "accursed"—devoted to the LORD. Its people and goods were not to be taken as plunder; metals went into the LORD's treasury. The Moabite Stone uses the same practice for a Moabite king's war on Israel.

Joshua 7.audience: Israel remembered the valley of Achor, where Achan was judged, by name; Hosea later promised it would become "a door of hope" (Hosea 2:15).

culture.title: A Babylonish garment
culture.text: A fine robe from Shinar (Babylonia) was a costly import, valued along with silver and a wedge of gold.

culture.title: Casting lots
culture.text: The guilty man was found by narrowing down tribe, clan, household, and individual, probably by lot. Lots were used to seek God's decision (Proverbs 16:33).

Joshua 8.audience: After taking Ai, Joshua leads Israel to Mount Ebal to carry out what Moses commanded (Deuteronomy 27). The law was read before men, women, children, and strangers (Joshua 8:35).

culture.title: Ambush tactics
culture.text: Drawing defenders out of a city with a feigned retreat while a hidden force enters it was a common ancient tactic. Israel uses it again at Gibeah (Judges 20:29–38).

culture.title: A heap of stones
culture.text: A heap of stones raised over the body of Ai's king remained "unto this day," as a visible landmark.

Joshua 9.audience: The Gibeonites lived among Israel for centuries as woodcutters and water carriers for the sanctuary (Joshua 9:27). Saul's later attack on them brought famine in David's day (2 Samuel 21:1–2).

culture.title: Worn-out wineskins
culture.text: Wine was carried in goatskin bags, which cracked with age. Old sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread made the Gibeonites look like travelers from far away.

culture.title: Treaties sworn by oath
culture.text: A treaty sworn in God's name could not be broken, even when it was found to rest on deception.

Joshua 10.audience: The five kings who attack Gibeon ruled cities in southern Canaan: Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. Hearers knew these as towns of Judah.

culture.title: The book of Jasher
culture.text: The text quotes the book of Jasher, a lost collection of poems. David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is also quoted from it (2 Samuel 1:18).

culture.title: Feet on the necks
culture.text: Putting a foot on a defeated enemy's neck was a common symbol of victory in ancient art, including Egyptian and Assyrian reliefs.

Joshua 11.audience: Hazor was the greatest city of northern Canaan—"the head of all those kingdoms" (Joshua 11:10). Hearers knew it later as a fortified city of Solomon (1 Kings 9:15).

culture.title: Hamstringing horses
culture.text: Cutting the tendons of the enemy's chariot horses made them useless for war. Israel did not keep chariot forces at this time.

culture.title: Cities on mounds
culture.text: Ancient cities were rebuilt on the ruins of earlier ones, forming mounds called tells. Israel did not burn the cities "that stood still in their strength"—on their mounds—except Hazor.

Joshua 12.audience: This list of defeated kings records the extent of the conquest east and west of the Jordan. Hearers would recognize many of the thirty-one cities as towns in their own land.

culture.title: City-state kings
culture.text: Canaan had many small kingdoms, each ruled from a walled city. Egyptian records of this era show the same pattern of local kings.

Joshua 13.audience: Joshua was old, and much land remained to be taken, including the Philistine cities on the coast (Joshua 13:1–3). Hearers knew the Philistines as long-term enemies.

culture.title: The Philistine five
culture.text: The Philistines had five chief cities—Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron—each ruled by a lord.

culture.title: No land for Levi
culture.text: Levi received no territory; the offerings made to the LORD were their inheritance.

Joshua 14.audience: Caleb's family were prominent in Judah. Hearers knew Hebron as their city, given to Caleb at age eighty-five (Joshua 14:10–14).

culture.title: Land by lot
culture.text: Each tribe's territory was assigned by lot, so the division was seen as God's decision rather than human favoritism.

Joshua 15.audience: This chapter describes Judah's territory and towns in detail. Judah became the leading tribe of the south, and Jerusalem lay on its northern border (Joshua 15:8).

culture.title: Springs as dowry
culture.text: Achsah asks her father for springs of water as well as land in the dry south. Water sources could make land valuable or worthless.

culture.title: Jebusites in Jerusalem
culture.text: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem. David later captured the city (2 Samuel 5:6–7).

Joshua 16.audience: Ephraim became the leading tribe of the north. Hearers knew that the Canaanites at Gezer remained among them as forced laborers (Joshua 16:10).

culture.title: Gezer
culture.text: Gezer guarded a key route from the coast into the hills. An Egyptian Pharaoh later captured it and gave it to Solomon as a dowry (1 Kings 9:16).

Joshua 17.audience: The tribe of Manasseh had land on both sides of the Jordan. The daughters of Zelophehad receive the inheritance promised in Numbers 27.

culture.title: Clearing forest
culture.text: The hill country was forested in ancient times. Joshua tells the house of Joseph to clear the woods to make room for settlement.

culture.title: Iron chariots
culture.text: Canaanites in the valleys had chariots fitted with iron. Chariots were effective on flat ground but not in the hills.

Joshua 18.audience: The tabernacle is set up at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), where it remained into Samuel's childhood (1 Samuel 1:3). Hearers knew Shiloh as Israel's early worship center.

culture.title: Surveying the land
culture.text: Three men from each tribe walked through the remaining land and wrote a description of it in seven parts in a book, before lots were cast.

Joshua 19.audience: The six remaining tribes receive their land here: Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan. Hearers knew that Simeon's towns lay within Judah (Joshua 19:1) and that Dan later moved north (Joshua 19:47).

culture.title: Joshua's town
culture.text: Joshua receives his own inheritance last, the town of Timnath-serah in Ephraim, which he rebuilt.

Joshua 20.audience: Six cities of refuge were named across the land so that anyone could reach one quickly. Hearers knew these towns: Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan.

culture.title: Trial at the gate
culture.text: The person fleeing stated his case to the elders at the city gate before being allowed in.

culture.title: Death of the high priest
culture.text: The manslayer stayed in the city until the death of the high priest, then could return home.

Joshua 21.audience: The Levites received forty-eight towns with pasturelands spread throughout the tribes (Joshua 21:41). Hearers would have had Levites living in or near their own region.

culture.title: Suburbs
culture.text: The KJV's "suburbs" means common pastureland around a town, used for grazing flocks.

Joshua 22.audience: The eastern tribes return home across the Jordan. Hearers knew the river as a natural barrier that could separate those tribes from the rest of Israel.

culture.title: An altar as a witness
culture.text: The eastern tribes build a large altar not for sacrifice but as a witness that they also belonged to the LORD. Israel's law allowed sacrifice only at the chosen place.

Joshua 23.audience: Joshua, "old and stricken in age" (Joshua 23:1), addresses Israel's elders, heads, judges, and officers. Hearers lived alongside the Canaanite nations that remained.

culture.title: Farewell speeches
culture.text: Leaders gave final addresses before death, as Moses and later Samuel and David did (1 Samuel 12; 1 Kings 2:1–4). Joshua says, "I am going the way of all the earth."

Joshua 24.audience: At Shechem, all the tribes renew the covenant. Joshua reminds them that their ancestors beyond the Euphrates "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2).

culture.title: A covenant written and witnessed
culture.text: Joshua writes the words in the book of the law and sets up a great stone under an oak as a witness. Treaties were written down and marked by memorials.

culture.title: Burials in the land
culture.text: Joshua, Joseph's bones, and Eleazar are all buried in the land of Ephraim. Joseph's bones rest at Shechem in the field Jacob bought (Genesis 33:19).
